capturing by "this" alone in a lambda context isn't safe.  Probably need to do the shared_from_this trick?  Or make scan somehow outlive the lifetime of FruDevice

`FruDevice` instance is in scope from beginning to end of `main` function.

You are right in a generic C++ context but in our particular case `FruDevice` is a singleton in the application context.

And when `FruDevice` instance goes out of scope we are already at the point where `fruDevice.io.run()` returns so there should not be any other code running beyond that point.

I am kind of stuck here as from a local reasoning perspective your suggestion is better but i would like to avoid introducing any `shared_ptr` for `FruDevice` instance since we know it's lifetime already (thus no need for `shared_ptr`).

So both choices are wrong and because of that i would like to go with the simpler choice (no `shared_ptr`).

Closing this discussion thread since there's been no further response in a week.

I would really like to avoid introducing additional `shared_ptr` if we can somehow avoid it.

> `FruDevice` instance is in scope from beginning to end of `main` function.

At this scope, that's not gauranteed that FruDevice and io_context are in the same scope, which leads to subtle bugs.

> 
> You are right in a generic C++ context but in our particular case `FruDevice` is a singleton in the application context.

Maybe I'm not understanding the term here.  This isn't a singleton, this is a stack variable declared in main, right?  

> 
> And when `FruDevice` instance goes out of scope we are already at the point where `fruDevice.io.run()` returns so there should not be any other code running beyond that point.

Right... this is the point, there's no guarantee of this within the class, which leads to subtle bugs.  FWIW, that's somewhat why these were globals initially and not on stack.

> 
> I am kind of stuck here as from a local reasoning perspective your suggestion is better but i would like to avoid introducing any `shared_ptr` for `FruDevice` instance since we know it's lifetime already (thus no need for `shared_ptr`).
> 
> So both choices are wrong and because of that i would like to go with the simpler choice (no `shared_ptr`).

> Maybe I'm not understanding the term here. This isn't a singleton, this is a stack variable declared in main, right? 

There's only ever a single instance of `FruDevice` class in the application.
~> singleton.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singleton_pattern

> In object-oriented programming, the singleton pattern is a software design pattern that restricts the instantiation of a class to a singular instance

I did not put a mechanism in the class to enforce it as singleton because i consider it to be obvious from looking at the usage within the application context.


> Right... this is the point, there's no guarantee of this within the class, which leads to subtle bugs. FWIW, that's somewhat why these were globals initially and not on stack.

And global vars accessible from any function which can see them does not lead to subtle bugs?

I posed the question about the general problem (is it ok to pass plain references to singleton objects) on discord
https://discordapp.com/channels/775381525260664832/867820390406422538/1436347622771130545
to get some more input on it.
I have moved to `shared_ptr` as suggested based on feedback received in discord.

> Right... this is the point, there's no guarantee of this within the class, which leads to subtle bugs. FWIW, that's somewhat why these were globals initially and not on stack.

Yes, there can be problems with classes that we do not have with globals.

I got one such issue in testing when `std::bind_front` was implicitly copy constructing the bus map.

Changed the code now to make the classes non-copyable and non-moveable.

This solidifies their role as singletons in the application context.
I hope this resolves your concern 👍
io_context should be shared separately from the fru portions itself.  this directory watcher really should know nothign about what a "fru" is ideally.

Yes but it was like that before with the global variables due to the wildcard capture. So i am not changing things here.

Having a class enables us to have encapsulation and do some OOP design but we don't necessarily have to do that right now.

If we start the fine grained encapsulation now we might open up some rabbit hole leading to further work which could bloat the diff and make this change harder to review.
closing this discussion thread since there's been no further response in a week.

> So i am not changing things here.

You've created the FruDevice class, so you've changed things.

The goal is not "fine grained" the goal is simplicity.  As written, now every API within fru device now could potentially be called from inotify.  At least with the global we have one variable.

> io_context should be shared separately from the fru portions itself. this directory watcher really should know nothign about what a "fru" is ideally.

Done, FruDevice now only stores a reference to io context. Sorry for getting stuck on this detail.
Should this just be owned within FruUtils?  Passing in a reference (even const) worries me that we'll get lifetime issues.
Sure. We can reach it via the class member then and do not need a reference anymore.
